title: Built an intraday trading bot — looking for feedback on a problem I’m struggling to solve
author: Fearless-Fold-1026
selftext:
I’ve been building and running my own **intraday equity trading bot** for Zerodha/Kite using Node.js.

The bot is fully automated and currently handles things like:

Market data and stock selection  
Signal generation  
Position sizing  
Automated order execution  
Dynamic position management  
Scaling into positions when a trade develops favourably  
Risk limits and maximum exposure controls  
Sector/exposure limits  
Different behaviour depending on market conditions  
Automated exits and end-of-day square-off  
Trade/state persistence and reconciliation  
Telegram notifications and monitoring  
Running continuously on a VPS with PM2

I’ve spent quite a lot of time fixing operational issues, and the system itself is now reasonably stable.

**But I’m facing a bigger problem at the strategy level.**  
The bot can identify a setup that looks good at the time of entry, and the trade initially meets the conditions I’m looking for. However, after entry, the market often becomes sideways or reverses.

So I’m seeing a pattern like:  
**Good-looking setup → entry → little/no follow-through → sideways/reversal → small loss**

The individual losses aren’t necessarily huge, but when this happens across multiple trades, **transaction costs + brokerage + repeated small losses** become a significant drag.  
I’ve deliberately designed the system to allow multiple opportunities rather than betting everything on one trade, but I’m now questioning whether that approach is appropriate for the current market environment.

I’d really appreciate opinions from people who have built or traded systematic intraday strategies.

A few things I’m particularly interested in:

How do you distinguish a genuinely failed setup from a setup that simply needs more time?

How do you deal with markets where there is plenty of intraday movement but poor follow-through?

How do you control the cost of taking multiple small trades?

What metrics do you use to determine whether the problem is the **entry**, **trade management**, or simply the **market regime**?

For those running automated intraday systems, what was the biggest lesson you learned after moving from backtesting to live trading?

I’m primarily looking for **practical experience and diagnostic ideas**, rather than someone trying to sell me a strategy.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
before changing anything, measure maximum favourable excursion on every one of those losers. that single distribution splits your problem in half.

if a decent share of them travel meaningfully in your favour before rolling over, your entry is fine and you have an exit problem. if most just sit there and never go anywhere, the signal has no follow-through in it, and no amount of position management invents some.

the cost drag deserves its own test. take the losing trades, set each one's result to zero, and see whether the system is still underwater. if it is, costs are not what is killing you, they are only the visible part.

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
Thanks, I actually ran the MFE analysis. interesting part is that 0.5%+ MFE trades behave very differently from the lower-MFE trades.

But this exposed the bigger problem: **I don’t currently know how to identify those high-follow-through trades at entry.**

I’ve looked at several entry-time characteristics, but haven’t found a clean separation between trades that develop and trades that stall.

I’ve recently added a two-stage confirmation step to test whether short-lived momentum is contributing to the problem, rather than changing multiple things at once.

I’ll also isolate transaction costs as you suggested.  
**If you’ve dealt with this before, I’d be particularly interested in how you determine whether a setup has enough potential follow-through before entering.**

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Checking MFE against every entry time variable I had was what settled it for me, and nothing separated cleanly.

That's a result too. If follow through isn't visible at entry then the fix sits on the exit instead. Time of day was the only thing that ever showed up.

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
That’s interesting — I haven’t specifically broken MFE down by time of day yet. I’ll test that before changing the strategy.  
If time-of-day is the only thing that shows a relationship in your experience, I’m curious whether you found a specific pattern in terms of *when* the follow-through tended to disappear.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
midday was the whole story for us. anything entered roughly 11 to 14 ET gave back most of its excursion, while the open and the last hour behaved like different instruments.

never got it down to a clean cutoff though, the boundary moved with how wide the open was. are you calling the open the first bar or the first 30 minutes?

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
I’m using 15-minute buckets rather than defining ‘the open’ as a single first bar. In my 343-trade sample, the strongest follow-through was roughly 9:30–10:30 IST, then MFE dropped sharply around 10:30–11:00.

Interestingly, I’m seeing something similar to what you describe: the boundary doesn’t look perfectly fixed. That’s why I’m testing time-of-day × market regime/opening expansion rather than simply hard-coding a 10:30 cutoff.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 343 trades spread over those buckets is maybe 20 to 30 each, so your 9:30-10:30 peak and the 10:30-11:00 drop overlap a lot more than the chart makes it look. Print n per bucket next to the MFE before you cross it with regime, because that cross cuts the counts again.

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body: Agreed. I’m looking at the bucket counts alongside MFE before doing any regime cross. The 343 trades are not evenly distributed, so I don’t want to overstate the 9:30–10:30 vs 10:30–11:00 difference. Once I cross with regime, the sample sizes get even smaller, so I’ll treat those results as directional unless the counts are large enough to support the conclusion.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: treating the regime cross as directional until the counts hold up is the right call. 343 split across time buckets and then across regimes stops being evidence pretty fast.

comments.author: Gibborish
comments.body: Sounds like perhaps the entry is just a signal and you need to add another gate for confirmation.  My bot only gets one chance per ticker, after one loss the ticker is blacklisted for 31 days.

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
Yeah, I already have multiple gates before an entry is allowed — market regime, stock-level momentum/confirmation, volume/liquidity and trend/VWAP checks, plus risk/exposure limits.

The bigger question I’m trying to answer is whether these gates are actually filtering for **future follow-through**, rather than simply confirming that the setup looks good at that moment. That’s what I’m testing now.

replies.author: tmc_void
replies.body: Gates are fine and all but do you have anything that continuously monitors and validates your position after the signal?

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
Yes, although it’s more lifecycle-based than a single continuous validation score. After entry I monitor velocity, acceleration, RVOL, momentum health, VWAP position, MFE/peak profit, market regime, and continuation. Those feed into things like continuation-failure, dead-trade, momentum deterioration, trailing/profit-lock and market risk-off exits.  
What I’m currently testing is whether that post-entry monitoring is reacting early enough. My MFE analysis suggests that’s probably the bigger issue: a large portion of losers never reach meaningful excursion, so I’m looking at whether I should invalidate those trades earlier rather than trying to optimize the entry gates further.

replies.author: tmc_void
replies.body: gotcha, that seems like a lot. depending on your strat, maybe pick 3 complementary and score based on if 2 agree, like vwap velocity atr or something. overgating or overfiltering can be problematic in it of itself, if feel like if you are heading down that direction, maybe the strat doesnt have an edge and is heavily dependent on the machinery around it. only time and testing will answer that question

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body: That’s a fair point. I’ve probably been heading toward too many gates, so I’m deliberately trying not to add more filters without evidence. My current focus is measuring whether the existing confirmation signals actually add incremental value, rather than stacking more conditions on top. The MFE analysis is pushing me more toward improving post-entry management than making the entry machinery more complicated. Ultimately, like you said, live testing and out-of-sample results will tell me whether there’s a real edge underneath it

comments.author: Realistic_Honey1177
comments.body: Did yu backtested your strategy? If yes yu can follow it in live market for atleast 3 month ,getting used to algotrading even though the backtest is good is a big process and it takes time.. hope you are backtested with correct data with no forward biased approach

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body:
Yes, I’ve backtested it, and I’m also running it live rather than assuming the backtest proves everything. I’ve been treating the live phase as a validation period because execution, slippage, liquidity and market regime can behave differently from historical data.  
I’m also specifically checking for forward-bias/look-ahead issues rather than just looking at the P&L. The current analysis is based on 343 closed live trades, and I’m using that data to identify where the strategy actually breaks down.  
The interesting finding so far is that the main problem doesn’t appear to be simply the entry signal — a lot of losing trades never develop meaningful MFE. So I’m testing the post-entry behaviour and execution side .

comments.author: presentofai
comments.body: if nothing at entry separates the followers from the chop, quit tuning the entry filter, that's a dead end. bank a partial at that 0.5% MFE band and trail the rest tight. lean on exits since follow-through clearly isn't predictable up front.

replies.author: Fearless-Fold-1026
replies.body: That’s pretty much where my data is pointing. In 343 closed trades, the entry metrics don’t cleanly separate the eventual winners from the chop, but MFE does — once a trade reaches around +0.5%, the outcome distribution changes dramatically. I’m testing whether that should trigger a different exit/position-management regime rather than continuing to tighten the entry filter. I’m not ready to assume a 0.5% partial is optimal yet, but the idea is definitely worth testing thanks

comments.author: Arez_G
comments.body: Guardas en alguna forma el contexto del trade qué ejecutas? Eso podría ayudarte a resolver la mayoría de problemática q mencionas
